items.title: I built the fastest & lightest AI coding agent GUI - 12MB, 4X FASTER, Fully Opensource!
items.summary:
Please Star PandaCode on GitHub: https://github.com/aicodeking/pandacode

Join this channel to get access to perks:
https://www.youtube.com/channel/@aicodeking/join

In this video, I'll show you PandaCode, a free and open-source desktop app I made that runs all your coding agents in one window: Claude Code, Codex, Kimi Code, OpenCode, GLM, MiMo, Grok Build and Antigravity, with the logins and plans you already pay for. I'll install it on Mac, Windows and Linux, tour the app, and send a real prompt with approvals, queued messages, steering and per-turn diffs, the Changes panel, the terminal and the built-in browser. Then we'll go through mobile simulators, attachments and moodboards, worktrees with two-click merges, GitHub, the task board, Agent Teams, Bots, local VMs and deploys. Finally, I'll cover Agent Usage, Resume at reset, the Token Saver, faster follow-ups, the Quick overlay, privacy, and the things that still need work.

--
Key Takeaways:

🐼 PandaCode runs Claude Code, Codex, K

items.title: These Claude Code Mods Are ACTUALLY Useful: Filetree, Replay Theater, Blast Radius & More
items.summary:
Join the membership (members-only videos on every level from Bronze up): https://www.youtube.com/@AICodeKing/join

In this video, I'll show you seven Claude Code mods that are actually useful, with the installation and a practical walkthrough for each one on a small task manager project. We start with Filetree, a file browser right next to the conversation, and Replay Theater, which lets you step through the edits Claude just made. Then we try Blast Radius on a dummy build folder, use Collision Guard with two chats editing the same file, and watch three parallel agents in Agent Flow. Finally, we save a reviewed project rule with Reflect and look at what Cache Tax can and can't do for your costs.

--
Key Takeaways:

⚙️ Mods need Claude Code 2.1.287 or newer, load by default, and run with your permissions, so check the publisher before installing.
📁 Filetree puts a project browser beside the conversation and shows which files Claude reads and changes, without a separate model request.
🎬

You can capture an instruction while it's fresh, but you're still responsible for deciding whether it's useful and where it belongs. This isn't retraining Claude. And writing a rule doesn't guarantee perfect obedience. It's maintaining an instruction file. So, keep the rules concise and revisit them when the project changes. Now, the last one is cash tax. And this needs a little more explanation because the money-saving angle is easy to oversell when Claude reuses a cashed conversation prefix that can be cheaper than writing that prefix into the cache again. Cash tax estimates the cost of returning to a cold conversation and it can make small requests to try to keep the existing prefix warm. To install it, add Karan Bansel's Claude Codemods marketplace, then install cash at claude codemods. Restart Claude afterward. Start with slashtags to inspect its information. For this demonstration, use /cashtags guard warn which changes the guard to a warning. The guard is intended for large conversations it estimates have gone cold. So don't expect every small test prompt to trigger it. For a limited warming window, you can use /kewarm 90mm that arms it for 90 minutes. A bare/ke keepwarm defaults to 6 hours, so I prefer being explicit while trying it. There is a major prerequisite here. Its normal 50-minute ping interval assumes a 1-hour conversation cache. subscription included. Usage currently uses that longer duration, while API key, usage credit, and cloud provider paths normally default to 5 minutes. If your actual cache expires after 5 minutes, a ping 50 minutes later doesn't keep it warm. Check the official caching settings for your provider before enabling this. The longer cache lifetime has a higher cash price. For a short functional demo, the project documents a 1 minute test interval. Send a small normal message first, then run/keepwarm1h everyone m keep claude open. Wait for a ping and inspect the reported usage. We're looking for evidence that the request reused cached input. When you've captured that run/ke keep warm off. Don't leave a rapid demonstration interval running after the test. A successful short ping still doesn't establish the savings from leaving a real conversation idle for an hour. That requires a longer check with the actual context provider and later request. I also ran the mods included automated tests. 56 passed. Those use a mocked engine and clock. So they check the mod's logic. They don't prove that a live server retained the cache or that my subscription allowance lasts longer. And the warming request itself costs tokens. It asks a model to reply. So there is input and output usage to account for. If you pay to keep warming a conversation and never come back to it, those requests didn't save you money on a later turn on a subscription. The dollar numbers are API equivalent estimates. They are not automatically an extra charge on your subscription bill and they are not a direct measurement of your remaining plan quota. Personally, I'd consider this for long conversations that I genuinely expect to resume for short sessions or a project I'm finished with. I wouldn't keep warming it just because a panel says I can. So, which of these would I start with? File Tree is an easy choice if you want to navigate a project without leaving the terminal. Replay theater is useful for reviewing small changes and blast radius gives you another checkpoint before the particular risky commands it recognizes for parallel work. Collision guard and agent flow solve different problems. overlapping file edits and visibility into the agents. Reflect is useful when repeated corrections should become reviewed project instructions. Cash tax is the one I'd evaluate most carefully against my actual usage. You don't need all seven running together. Start with the problem you actually have. install that mod and check its behavior on a small project. You can disable a mod from the installed section of /plugin if it isn't earning its place. Overall, this is the direction I like for Claude Code mods. Useful controls around real coding work with results you can inspect yourself. Overall, it's pretty cool. Anyway, let me know your thoughts in the comments. If you like this video, consider donating through the super thanks option or becoming a member by clicking the join button. Also, give this video a thumbs up and subscribe to my channel. I'll see you in the next one. Until then, bye.

items.title: Opus + Sol Orchestrated Team: This BEATS every AI MODEL right now! (Tested)
items.summary:
Join this channel to get access to perks:
https://www.youtube.com/channel/@aicodeking/join

In this video, I'll test five AI coding teams in Bambooed, where one model leads and plans the work while another handles the assignments: Opus 5.5 with GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Astra with Sonnet 5.5, Opus with Sonnet, Astra with Sol, and Opus with Muse Wonder Full. I'll explain the setup and then go through the six KingBench 4 tasks (the emulator, the Docker alternative, the 3D room designer, the QMK keyboard configurator, the Pokémon opening and the Fitbit desktop app), showing the team conversations, the apps themselves and where the teamwork helped or failed. After that, I look at the overall scores, the recorded tokens and costs, and what those numbers can and can't tell you. Finally, I tell you which lead-and-worker setup I'd start with and what I'd check before letting workers loose on my next project.

--
Key Takeaways:

👥 Five lead-and-worker teams ran all six KingBench 4 tasks through Bamboo
items.author: AICodeKing
items.transcript: Hi. Welcome to another video. So, I tested five AI teams to see which lead and worker setup I'd actually use for a coding project. One model plans the work and checks the results, while another handles the assignments. That's orchestration, and the lead's decisions can shape the whole application. I followed their conversations and tested the applications. So, let's see where the teamwork helped and where it failed. The models are Opus 5.5, GPT 6.1, Soul, GPT 6, Astra, Sonnet 5.5, and Muse Wonderful 1. The five pairs are Opus with Soul, Astra with Sonnet, Opus with Sonnet, Astra with Soul, and Opus with Museful. The first model is always the lead. Everything ran through Bambood using Claude Code, Codex, and the native Muse CLI. Each team had up to three simultaneous workers, 20 lead rounds, and 50 assignments without an added time limit. The six tasks were an emulator, Docker alternative, Room Designer, Keyboard Configurator, Pokémon Opening, and Fitbit Desktop App. Each task was worth 10 points. Each pair gets one high-effort run per task on a shared machine without equal computation budgets. There are no matched solo tests or reversed roles, so this comparison doesn't isolate how much delegation itself helps. The emulator asks for Game Boy, DS, and 3DS support in Rust, including saving and normal playback features. Both Astra-led teams planned Game Boy execution, but only file inspection for DS and 3DS, leaving those execution paths missing. Astra with Sonnet gets 1.9 out of 10, and Astra with Soul gets 2.2. But, improving Game Boy support doesn't make a DS file inspector run DS game. Opus with Soul earns 6.2 with connected execution paths for all three systems. DS and 3DS examples demonstrate rendering with separate 3DS input checks. Opus with Sonnet earns 7.1, the highest emulator score. It passes all eight shared Game Boy diagnostics and the Game Boy Color City Builder supports useful controls and saving. The DS and 3DS examples also progress further, although these small homebrew tests don't prove that most commercial games work. Opus with Muse full earns 5.8 with some output across all three systems, but blank or incomplete results in broader examples. Provider quota errors interrupt workers and the lead completes more of the work. So, Opus with Sonnet produces the strongest emulator here. While the Astra teams show how an incomplete plan limits everything that followed. For the Docker alternative, importing an image is only part of the job. You also need process isolation and resource controls and these macOS hosted reviews didn't establish working isolation through the delivered Linux paths. That limits the scores to five even where the image tools work. Opus with Soul, Opus with Sonnet, and Astra with Sonnet all get 5.0. Astra with Soul gets 4.7 with working registry and Docker save workflows, but no import for the standard OCI archive format. None of the teams demonstrates the requested efficiency advantage over Docker. Opus with Muse full gets 3.0 after an extraction test, changes permissions on two owned directories outside the intended extraction route. Their contents stay unchanged and both remain inside the application storage parent. This doesn't demonstrate a guest escaping Linux or overriding arbitrary host files. That run also suffers quota interruptions and none of these results establishes a complete Docker replacement. The room designer produces much more usable applications. In the Opus and Soul project, a tester finds that selecting a chair makes the viewport go blank. The lead suspects an old builder screenshot problem, but the tester reproduces the failure. A worker repairs the selection highlight and the lead checks the rebuilt app. That's the kind of review loop I want from a team. Opus with Soul earns 8.9 while Opus with Sonnet and Astra with Soul both earn 9.0. The Opus and Sonit version still lets oversized furniture protrude from a smaller room. Opus with Muse full earns 8.9 with custom shapes, colored lighting, and working project restoration. Color changes leave three extra textures retained, although normal editions followed by undo remain stable. This run finishes without an observed quota failure, even though its usage records still have gaps. Astra with Sonit earns 9.3, the highest room score. The lead gives the room model, editor, and renderer separate owners, then sends specific corrections as those parts connect. Editing and project restoration work and repeated object additions and removals return to the original resource counts. A very thin object can overhang the wall slightly, but this is the room designer I'd favor from these results. The keyboard task asks for a yellow themed alternative to VA that configures QMK keyboards. A nice editor isn't enough if the keyboard never receives the changes. I checked configuration messages and resulting state through an independently controlled virtual keyboard. That's limited compatibility evidence, not proof of support for every physical keyboard or firmware version. Opus with Soul earns 7.8 and Opus with Sonit earns 7.4. Both send configuration messages that change the tested device state with editing compatibility and backup limitations reducing their scores. Both Astra lead versions earn 2.8 and their assignments explain why. Astra with Soul assigns selection and metadata, while Astra with Sonit explicitly excludes opening the device and sending configuration messages. The benchmark prohibited changing real connected hardware, but it didn't prohibit implementing that communication path. So, the teams improve local editors while the required connection remains absent. Opus with Muse full earns 7.7 with working keycodes, macros, lighting, and restoration in a fresh browser profile. It still accepts an incomplete acknowledgement and invalid macro imports can partly change the configuration. Quota failures also interrupt the workers before the lead completes further repairs. Opus with Sol leads this task, and the bigger lesson is to include the device connection before spending more work on appearance. For Pokémon, I wanted an ordinary playable opening through the first gym with progress that survives saving and loading. Opus with Sol earns 8.6, and Opus with Sonnet earns 8.7. Both complete that route when browser storage works, but change names, simpler artwork, and simplified mechanics reduce fidelity. The credited tests use ordinary play, not the agents' heavily leveled parties or automatic healing. Opus with Museful scores zero because it delivers no playable game. There is a contract and a graphics helper, but no entry point, world battles, or saving. Subscription quota errors affect all six workers used during the run, eventually blocking even a request to read one line and reply. That zero describes the delivered project, not what Muse could do with available capacity. Astro with Sonnet earns 9.1, the highest Pokémon score. The lead catches a walk-through that tells players to heal Imputer without providing a healing center. It assigns the missing door, nurse, and return route. The independent route completes the parcel quest, catches a wild Pokémon, and reaches Brock through the forest. Normal losses have the money and give no badge, while winning from a legitimate save awards the badge and expected money. Progress survives another reload when storage works. It's still a reduced game without evolution or move use limits. A misleading save success message when storage is blocked also costs points because reloading loses that temporary checkpoint. Astro with Sol also scores zero with a completely empty folder after an HTTP 429 error exhausts retries. The logs don't establish whether account quota or another rate limit caused it. Astro with Sonnet leads the completed game comparison, while those interrupted runs need working provider access before we can judge their full potential. The Fitbit task asks for a desktop analytics app with a Rust back end. Opus with Soul earns 7.7, while Opus with Sonnet earns 6.5. Soul's provider clients work against controlled test inputs representing expected provider responses, while Sonnet's external connection receives credit from source inspection only. Neither result establishes a personal Fitbit account connection or clinical accuracy. In the Opus and Sonnet app, a workout's calculated load can appear in its detail view, but disappear from the daily summary. In the Opus and Soul app, demo data replaces imported daily measurements, and clearing the demo removes those days. Importing the original synthetic CSV again restores the exact values, so the demonstrated loss is recoverable. Opus with Muse full earns 6.3 with substantive Rust calculations, but broken connect and import buttons that fail before reaching the back end. Direct back end calls don't fix those broken buttons. This run also suffers quota interruptions. Both Astro led health apps earn 7.6. Astro with Sonnet catches demo refresh deleting user records. A worker also finds an old interface inside the package tab, so the lead rebuilds it and checks the embedded files. A repaired source file doesn't help if you launch an older packet. Its final app supports workout and journal entries with data surviving export, import, and restart, but it accepts only its own JSON format without a Fitbit connection or actual Fitbit export path. Its load calculation treats missing days as zero, so incomplete history can produce misleading results. Astro with Soul repairs retries that could create duplicate workouts after a lost response. An independent test loses that response, then retries after reopening the dialogue, and exactly one workout remains. The pending draft still doesn't survive an application reload. That app also relies on its own JSON format rather than a working Fitbit connection. It shows zero steps on a workout only date and renders a thousand workouts as a thousand table rows. The Astra health checks use the rust services in a browser, so the complete native desktop experience remains unverified. Opus with Soul leads this task, but every result still has gaps against the requested product. Now, here's the overall result. Opus with Soul earns 44.2 out of 60 or 73.67%. Opus with Sonnet follows at 43.7 or 72.83% with five quota affected tasks. Astra with Soul earns 26.3 or 43.83% including its interrupted Pokémon run. I keep those delivered scores visible, but the interruptions prevent a fair capability ranking across all five teams. These percentages measure earned points, not future success rate. For tokens and cost, the totals include leads, workers, corrections, and recorded additional model calls. Setup and evaluation are excluded. Resumed usage counts only once and missing records remain unknown. The total is about 936.11 million recorded tokens including 926.74 million input and 9.37 million output. Most input is repeated cached context and reasoning already belongs to output, so it doesn't count twice. Opus with Sonnet records about 444.81 million tokens compared with 143.73 million for Opus with Soul. Astra with Sonnet records 107.06 million, Opus with Muse full records 155.06 million, and Astra with Soul records 85.45 million. These counts include repeated context and don't directly measure useful code. Using the saved API rates, Soul and Sonnet each cost $2 for fresh input, 0.10 for cached reads, and $10 for output per million tokens. Opus costs $4.20 and $20 for those categories, while Astra cost $10, $1 and $0.50. So, Opus is twice Soul's unit price, while Astra is five times its fresh input and output price, and 10 times its cached read price. Cash write and long context rules also affect the calculations. For Muse full, I used the requested standard wonder assumption, $4 for fresh input, $0.20 for cached reads, and $20 for output. That isn't a confirmed full tariff or subscription invoice. And there is no confirmed full cash rate right here. For the subtotals, native Claude cost records replace the Claude token estimates where available with token estimates for the other providers. Those alternatives don't get added together, and the records don't establish every hosted fee. Opus with Soul records about $56.97, while Opus with Sonnet records $124.22. Astra with Sonnet records $68.75. Opus with Muse full records $80.22, and Astra with Soul records $75.22. That's about $405.49 of recorded orchestration usage, but only eight of the 30 tasks have complete captured usage. Every team's final cost remains unknown, so these subtotals can't identify the cheapest setup or a score per dollar winner. A lower recorded amount can also mean some usage is missing. For my own starting setup, I'd choose Opus leading Soul. It has the highest comparable total and stays useful across all six tasks, with Opus leading Sonnet a close alternative. I'd favor the Sonnet team for emulation, while Soul's team scores higher on the keyboard and health applications. Astra with Sonnet is worth considering for the visual editor and small game work demonstrated here. But, I'd inspect its initial assignments carefully because its emulator and keyboard plans omit required work. Opus with Muse full and Astra with Soul need complete runs before I'd make a fair overall comparison. For my next project, I'd check that every required feature has an owner before the workers start. Then I'd reproduce disputed failures, test the normal user journey, and check the final package. More runs and complete costs are still needed before making broader reliability or value claims. Overall, it's pretty cool. Anyway, let me know your thoughts in the comments. If you like this video, consider donating through [music] the Super Thanks option or becoming a member by clicking the join button. Also, give this [music] video a thumbs up and subscribe to my channel. I'll see you in the next one. Until then, bye. >> [music]

In this video, I'll show you pstack, the open-source skill collection from poteto, who works at Cursor and on the React core team, and how to adapt it for Claude Code. I'll have Claude install and adapt the skills, then use /poteto-mode on a real search bug: it reproduces the failure, throws out a theory the evidence disproves, writes a failing test, makes a small fix and repeats the same interaction to prove it works. After that, I'll use how, why and teach to understand the code, then build an export feature with architect, arena, swarm and interrogate. Finally, I'll cover finish conditions for longer work, the cost tradeoff and my take.

--
Key Takeaways:

🧠 pstack is an open-source (MIT) collection of skills from poteto that pushes Claude to investigate before editing, keep fixes small and check the result works.
💻 It was built for Cursor, but you can have Claude Code adapt the skills for your project, your tools and your models.
🎯 /poteto-mode is the main entry point: give it the
items.author: AICodeKing
items.transcript: [music] >> Hi, welcome to another video. So, [music] you ask Claude code to fix a bug. It edits a bunch of files, runs the tests, and says it's fixed. You open the app, same bug, or you ask for an export button, and somehow you've got a new framework to maintain. P stack is a collection of skills that pushes Claude to investigate before editing, keep the fix small, and check that the thing you asked for actually works. It also gives you ways to compare designs, split up investigations, and get another agent to review the result. It comes from Potato, who works at Cursor and on the React core team. These are the skills she uses in her own engineering workflow, and they're open source under the MIT license. They were built for Cursor, but you can adapt the instructions for Claude code or another coding agent with skills or custom rules. We're focusing on Claude code here, so let's get right into it. For setup, open Claude code in your project and give it the P stack repo linked below. Ask it to adapt the skills for your project, preserve your existing instructions, use the tools and models available, and check that everything works. Have it tell you if anything else is needed. Let Claude handle the compatibility changes. Once it's checked the setup, your main entry point is {slash} potato-mode. Give it the task and a clear description of what a working result looks like. The playbooks guide it through the steps. Here's an example. You've got a search box, and when you type quickly, the results sometimes jump back to an older search. I'd say {slash} potato-mode, reproduce the search bug in the running app, find the cause, make the smallest fix, and verify the same interaction afterward. Leave the changes ready for review. The bug fix playbook tells Claude to reproduce the failure before choosing a fix. In this example, it should watch the requests and check which response updates the page. Maybe an older request finishes late and overwrites the newer results. That's something Claude needs to confirm. If the evidence points elsewhere, it needs to follow it. And I really like this detail. If Claude tries something and the evidence disproves its theory, the playbook tells it to remove the changes based on that theory. Otherwise, a debugging session can leave you with five workarounds and no idea which one helped. Once it finds the cause, capture a failing test if there's a cheap way to do it, then make the fix. Finally, repeat the original interaction. Make that older request finish late and check that the newest search still wins. That's what I'd want to see before accepting the patch. Show me the failure, explain the cause, and show me the same thing working afterward. Now, sometimes you need Claude to understand the code before you even know what to change. That's where how, why, and teach come in. With {slash} how, you could ask, "How do search filters get from this form into the database query?" Claude traces the code and explains the flow. Useful when you've opened a project and have no idea where anything lives. {slash} why digs into the reasons behind the code using the history and evidence it can access. Say there's a retry limit that looks arbitrary. Ask why it was added before telling Claude to remove it. There may be a reason that isn't obvious from the function itself. Then use {slash} teach when you want to understand the answer yourself. After the search fix, ask Claude to explain how the requests got out of order and why this change prevents it. I like that for learning while building. You can ask follow-up questions until you understand the code you're going to maintain. Now, let's add that export button. Use {slash} architect and say, "Design an export feature that downloads the currently filtered results." Show how the page, API, and export code fit together before implementing it. This gets Claude to work through the decisions early. Which filters apply? How much data could this return? Can we reuse the existing query? You want those answers before it has written half the feature. Piece stacks principles also push it to keep the solution small. For a simple dashboard, reusing what you've already built might be enough. I don't want a new job system unless the export actually needs one. If there's a design choice worth comparing, use Arena. Arena sends the same task to multiple agents and has them produce independent candidates. The lead compares them, gets another judgment, picks a base, and brings over useful ideas from the other attempts. Then it checks the combined result. For the export, you could compare returning the file directly with preparing it in a background job. Give both attempts the same requirements and see how they handle the expected data size, complexity, and user experience. This is useful when Claude's first idea sounds plausible, but you'd like to see another approach before committing to it. Swarm helps when the work can be split up. One agent could trace the back-end filters, another could inspect the filter state on the page, and a third could check the existing tests. Each gets a specific job, and the lead brings their findings together. You can do the same across packages in a larger repo. You get one report with the issues found and any parts the agents couldn't verify. That last bit matters. An unfinished check shouldn't quietly turn into a pass. Once Claude has built the export, use /interrogate to review it. Ask the reviewers to check whether it respects the selected filters and handles failures properly. Interrogate gets independent reviews, then assesses the findings. Which issues could break the feature? Which suggestions are worth considering? Which complaints are wrong or missing context? I like that it asks the lead agent to make those calls. AI reviews can generate a lot of extra work if you treat every suggestion as a requirement. This skill gives you a review verdict without automatically applying every proposed change. Use the models available in your Claude code setup for those roles. Another reviewer can catch something the author missed, but you still need to check the actual feature. For our export, apply a filter, download the file, and inspect the rows and columns. A successful build doesn't tell you whether the file contains the right data. You don't need all of them for every little edit. A small bug might only need reproduction, a focused fix, and a check in the app. For longer work, give Claude a finished condition it can keep checking. If you're migrating an API, that could mean every caller uses the new version, the old API is removed, and the relevant tests pass. Ask it to keep a decision log and leave a checkpoint if the work needs another session. That gives you something specific to review when you come back. There is a cost trade-off, though. The skill files are open source, but extra agents and review rounds still use your Claude code allowance or API budget. If you're watching your usage, start with one implementation and one focused review. Save the bigger comparisons for decisions where another attempt could help. My take is that Pstack is worth trying if you keep reminding Claude to reproduce bugs and check the app before saying it's done. Having those expectations written into the skills gives you something you can reuse and adjust. Give it a task you understand well, and look at what comes back. I judge it by the patch and the checks it ran. The repository is linked below if you want to adapt it for Claude code or the coding agent you prefer. Overall, it's pretty cool. Anyway, let me know your thoughts in the comments. >> [music] >> If you like this video, consider donating through the Super Thanks option or becoming a member by clicking the join button. Also, give this video [music] a thumbs up and subscribe to my channel. I'll see you in the next one. Until then, bye. >> [music] [music]

items.title: RIP Reverse Engineer Anything! This 8 KB Skill Outperforms REA (38% Faster)
items.summary:
Join this channel to get access to perks:
https://www.youtube.com/channel/@aicodeking/join

Star LeanREA here: https://github.com/aicodeking/leanrea

In this video, I'll show you LeanREA, a single 8 KB skill file that I built to do the same job as REA (Reverse Engineer Anything) without an MCP server or any extra tools. I explain what REA is under the hood, then go through what is inside the skill: the rules, the router table that maps each target type to its fastest command, and the ready-to-run first moves. Then I show my benchmark in Claude Code with Sonnet 5.5 across 36 runs, where LeanREA was 38% faster and 35% cheaper than REA at the same accuracy, plus the context test and a tool-by-tool speed test. I also talk about the limits of the benchmark, two bugs I found in my own skill, and how to install it with one npx skills command.

--
Key Takeaways:

📦 LeanREA is one 8 KB skill file with no MCP server and no extra tools; the agent runs the real tools in its normal shell.
🔀 REA is
items.author: AICodeKing
items.transcript: Hi. Welcome to another video. Before starting the video, I have been posting many tutorials of open source projects that I like in members only videos as well. I am posting more regularly. So, if you want to support the channel, please hit the join button and the videos are available on all tiers from bronze and up. So, please go ahead and check them out. Now, back to the video. So, in my last video I talked about REA. REA means reverse engineer anything. It is a very popular project on GitHub. In that video, I said that REA is not that useful. I said that models can already do this work with the normal tools on your machine and I said that a small skill file can do the same job. Some people asked me to prove it, so I built it. I call it lean REA. It is one skill file. It is about 8 kilobytes. And in my benchmark, it was 38% faster than REA and 35% cheaper with the same accuracy. So, let's get right into it. First, let's remember what REA is. REA is an MCP server and a CLI. It puts 207 tools into your agent. The NPM package is about 25 megabytes and the skill files with all the reference docs are about 72 kilobytes. Under the hood, REA mostly calls tools that you already have. For an electron app, it uses the ASAR package. For a Mac binary, it uses Otool and NM. For a Go binary, it reads the same build info that Go version {dash} M reads. For Android, it uses Jadx and APKTool. So, REA is a layer on top of the same tools. Lean REA removes that layer. There is no MCP server. There are no extra tools. The agent uses its normal shell and it runs the real tools directly. Now, let's talk about what is inside the skill file. To make it, I went through the REA source code. I mapped each REA feature to the plain command that does the same thing. Then I kept only the fastest command for each target. The first part is a short list of rules. Work on a copy of the target. Check the file type first. Do not read a big minified file, search inside it and read only the part that you need and put many small checks into one shell call. The second part is a router. It is a table. On the left, you have the type of target. On the right, you have the fastest command for It covers electron apps, minified web bundles, and Mac, Linux, and Windows binaries. It covers Go, Rust, .NET, Android APKs, and Flutter. And it also covers WASM, SQLite files, packet captures, firmware, and websites. The third part is what I call first moves. These are ready commands that the agent can paste and run. For a Mac binary, one command gets the linked libraries, the exports, the imports, the strings, and the full list of functions. All of it in one call. And this matters a lot because with agents, each turn costs time. A turn is one round trip between the model and a tool. Fewer turns means a faster answer. The skill also keeps the useful tricks that are inside the REA code. For example, how to read the electron fuses, how to find the Go build info in a binary, how to find the Flutter snapshot hash. These are small details, but the model can miss them. So, they are in the file. And it has simple evidence rules. The model marks each claim as seen, inferred, or unknown. If it did not find a fact, it says unknown. It does not say that the thing is absent. That is the whole skill. The REA skill docs are about nine times bigger. Now, let's talk about the benchmark because this is the important part. I used Claude code in headless mode with Sonic 5.5. I made three setups. The first setup is no skill and no MCP, just the model and its normal tools. The second setup is Lean REA. The third setup is REA. That means the REA MCP server plus the official REA skill. Then, I made four tasks. The first task uses a real electron desktop app. The model must trace one feature through the app code. It must find the native function, the class that controls it, and the IPC channels. IPC is how the parts of an electron app talk to each other. The second task uses the native add-on from that same app. It is a small Mac binary. The model must list the exports, explain one permission check, and explain how the single instance lock work. >> The third task is a Go binary. I used the GitHub CLI. The model must find the Go version and the versions of two dependencies. The fourth task is the hard one. It uses the same native add-on, but this time the model must read the disassembly. It must find the exact path of a socket file, the wire protocol, and how the app checks who is connecting. Each setup did each task three times. So, that is 36 runs in total. I checked every answer against an answer key that I made by hand. And here are the results. Lean REA finished all the runs in 388 seconds. With no skill, it took 479 seconds. And REA took 627 seconds. For cost, Lean REA was $2.17. No skill was $2.21. And REA was $3.36. For turns, Lean REA used 55 turns. No skill used 81. And REA used 124.
